pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:50 — Create/Update/Delete each spawn an independent unsynchronized goroutine to write Legacy, so a client doing Create then immediate Delete (or Update) on the same name has no ordering guarantee between the two legacy goroutines — a fast Delete's legacy goroutine can finish before a slower Create's legacy goroutine, leaving a permanent "ghost" object in Legacy that Storage no longer has, with zero error or signal.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:50 — None of the four fire-and-forget goroutines (Create:50-57, Delete:108-114, Update:134-141, DeleteCollection:161-167) wrap d.Legacy.<Method> in a recover(); an unrecovered panic in any of them crashes the entire apiserver process (Go terminates the whole program on an unrecovered goroutine panic), turning a single bad legacy-store response into a full outage instead of a per-request error.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:45 — When d.Storage.Create fails, the error path calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) instead of d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...) (Legacy was never even attempted) — pure Storage outages get attributed to the Legacy-failure metric while the Storage-failure metric never fires, so an on-call dashboard/alert keyed on Storage failures stays green during a real Storage outage and instead falsely implicates Legacy.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:129 — Same bug as Create: when d.Storage.Update fails, d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) is called instead of d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...), so Storage.Update failures are invisible to Storage metrics and falsely reported as Legacy failures, misdirecting incident response during an actual Storage-side outage.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:36 — Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection now return success to the caller the instant Storage succeeds, before the Legacy goroutine even starts; there is no response field, event, status condition, or retry/reconciliation mechanism exposing legacy-store failure or divergence to the caller or to any consumer of the object — every write reports success even when Legacy is now permanently out of sync, which is a systemic silent-pass by design, not just a bug in one path.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:106 — d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes the object `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind` for the "kind" label — this mislabels the Delete success metric with an unbounded-cardinality object name instead of resource kind, breaking dashboard aggregation by kind and risking Prometheus cardinality blowup under high delete volume.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go:189 — TestMode3_Delete never configures a Legacy mock expectation ("Delete" is never registered on the shared mock.Mock) even though Delete now fires a detached goroutine calling d.Legacy.Delete — the goroutine either races an unconfigured testify mock call after the subtest has already returned (potential panic invisible to the reported test result) or simply never gets scheduled before the process moves on, so the test proves nothing about whether legacy deletion actually happens and stays green either way.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3_test.go:243 — Same gap as the Delete test: TestMode3_DeleteCollection sets up no Legacy mock expectation for "DeleteCollection", so the async legacy goroutine's behavior (success, failure, or an unconfigured-mock panic) is completely unverified and invisible to the test outcome — CI is green regardless of whether legacy collection deletion is broken.

pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:50 — There is no bound, semaphore, or backpressure on the number of concurrent detached legacy-write goroutines; because Storage now returns success independent of Legacy's capacity/latency, a client (malicious or just bursty) can fire an unbounded number of rapid Create/Update/Delete requests and cause an unbounded number of concurrent in-flight connections/goroutines against the Legacy store with no feedback to the caller that Legacy is falling behind or failing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:45 — On Storage.Create failure the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration instead of d.recordStorageDuration, misattributing a unified-storage write failure to the legacy-store metric series

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go Create(), the Storage.Create error path calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the timed operation (`startStorage`) and the failure are for the unified Storage write. adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:51 — The fire-and-forget Legacy.Create goroutine derives its 10s timeout context from the request-scoped ctx; once the HTTP handler returns (immediately after Create returns) that context is typically canceled by net/http, aborting the "async" legacy write almost immediately instead of allowing the intended 10s window

adjudication.rationale: In DualWriterMode3.Create, the legacy write is launched in a goroutine and its timeout context is derived from the passed-in `ctx` (`context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...)`). Since Create returns immediately after starting the goroutine, any cancellation of the parent `ctx` by the caller will also cancel the legacy write before the intended 10s window. The diff doesn’t prove the caller is an HTTP request context, but the code clearly couples the async operation’s lifetime to the request-scoped context, which can undermine the “fire-and-forget with 10s timeout” intent.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:110 — Same request-context timeout issue as Create: the Legacy.Delete goroutine's 10s deadline is derived from the request-scoped ctx, which is likely already canceled once the handler returns, defeating the fire-and-forget design

adjudication.rationale: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the legacy delete is executed in a goroutine with `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...)` where `ctx` is the incoming request context (re-wrapped only with logging). If the caller cancels that context when the handler returns (typical for request-scoped contexts), the derived timeout context will already be canceled, causing the “fire-and-forget” legacy delete to abort immediately and potentially leaving LegacyStorage out of sync with Storage.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:129 — On Storage.Update failure the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration instead of d.recordStorageDuration, same storage/legacy metric mislabeling bug as in Create

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:135 — Same request-context timeout issue: the Legacy.Update fire-and-forget goroutine derives its timeout from the request-scoped ctx instead of a detached background context, so it is likely canceled before the intended 10s elapses

adjudication.rationale: In `DualWriterMode3.Update`, the legacy write is executed in a fire-and-forget goroutine that does `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...)` where `ctx` is the request-scoped context passed into `Update` (and stored in the closure). If the request context is canceled when the main request completes, the derived timeout context will be canceled immediately, so the intended 10s grace period for `d.Legacy.Update(...)` likely won’t elapse and the legacy update can be skipped prematurely. This behavior is directly shown in the diff (same pattern also appears in Create/Delete/DeleteCollection).

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:139 — Update no longer resolves the object via Storage.Get + objInfo.UpdatedObject and wraps the resolved object for Legacy.Update (the removed updateWrapper logic); it now forwards the client's original objInfo unchanged, so Legacy.Update independently recomputes its own "updated" object from Legacy's own (potentially divergent/stale) old object instead of the object actually persisted to Storage, breaking dual-store consistency guarantees

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, Update previously did Storage.Get + objInfo.UpdatedObject and used updateWrapper to ensure Legacy.Update was applied using the same resolved/updated object that was written to Storage. The new implementation calls d.Storage.Update(..., objInfo, ...) and then asynchronously calls d.Legacy.Update(..., objInfo, ...) with the original objInfo unchanged. This means Legacy.Update will derive its update from Legacy’s own current/old object, which can diverge from Storage’s old object, so the two stores may end up with different updated results for the same request, breaking the prior consistency behavior implied by the removed wrapper logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:163 — Same request-context timeout issue: the Legacy.DeleteCollection goroutine derives its timeout from the request-scoped ctx, likely canceled before the intended 10s elapses

adjudication.rationale: In DualWriterMode3.DeleteCollection, the legacy delete is executed in a goroutine using `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...)` where `ctx` is the request-scoped context passed into DeleteCollection (and already wrapped with `klog.NewContext`). If the request context is canceled/returns before 10s, the derived context will be canceled immediately and the legacy delete may not complete, undermining the intended 10s timeout and potentially skipping the legacy-side delete.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:50 — Create/Update/Delete each spawn an independent unsynchronized goroutine to write Legacy, so a client doing Create then immediate Delete (or Update) on the same name has no ordering guarantee between the two legacy goroutines — a fast Delete's legacy goroutine can finish before a slower Create's legacy goroutine, leaving a permanent "ghost" object in Legacy that Storage no longer has, with zero error or signal.

adjudication.rationale: In pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go, Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection all perform the Unified Store operation synchronously, then fire-and-forget a legacy write in an unsynchronized goroutine (e.g., Create: `go func(){ d.Legacy.Create(...) }()`, Delete: `go func(){ d.Legacy.Delete(...) }()`, Update similarly). There is no per-object serialization or ordering between these goroutines. Therefore, a client doing Create then immediate Delete/Update on the same name can have the legacy goroutines execute out of order (e.g., legacy Delete runs first and returns NotFound, then legacy Create runs and succeeds), leaving a "ghost" object in Legacy while Storage has deleted it, with no surfaced error (legacy errors are only recorded via metrics). This behavior is directly implied by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:50 — None of the four fire-and-forget goroutines (Create:50-57, Delete:108-114, Update:134-141, DeleteCollection:161-167) wrap d.Legacy.<Method> in a recover(); an unrecovered panic in any of them crashes the entire apiserver process (Go terminates the whole program on an unrecovered goroutine panic), turning a single bad legacy-store response into a full outage instead of a per-request error.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces multiple fire-and-forget goroutines in pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go that call d.Legacy.<Method> (Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection) without any defer/recover wrapper. In Go, an unrecovered panic in any goroutine will crash the entire process. Because these legacy writes are now executed in separate goroutines, any panic inside d.Legacy.* cannot be caught by any per-request recovery that might exist on the request-handling goroutine, turning a legacy-store panic into a full apiserver crash. This crash risk is directly visible in the new `go func(){ ... d.Legacy.*(...) ... }()` blocks.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:36 — Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection now return success to the caller the instant Storage succeeds, before the Legacy goroutine even starts; there is no response field, event, status condition, or retry/reconciliation mechanism exposing legacy-store failure or divergence to the caller or to any consumer of the object — every write reports success even when Legacy is now permanently out of sync, which is a systemic silent-pass by design, not just a bug in one path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly changes Mode3 write paths to return based solely on Unified Store success and perform the Legacy write asynchronously in a goroutine (e.g., `Create` spawns `go func(){ d.Legacy.Create(...) }()` after `d.Storage.Create` and returns `created, err`; similarly for `Update`, `Delete`, and `DeleteCollection`). There is no propagation of legacy errors to the caller and no explicit reconciliation/retry mechanism shown in this diff—legacy failures are at most recorded via `recordLegacyDuration(...)` (and in `DeleteCollection` the goroutine even calls `recordStorageDuration(...)`), so divergence can be silent from the API consumer’s perspective. However, since Mode3 semantics/contract aren’t fully specified in the diff and the previous implementation already did not fail the request on legacy-write errors (it logged but returned success), this is best treated as an architectural/behavioral concern introduced/expanded by the async change rather than a strictly verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go:50 — There is no bound, semaphore, or backpressure on the number of concurrent detached legacy-write goroutines; because Storage now returns success independent of Legacy's capacity/latency, a client (malicious or just bursty) can fire an unbounded number of rapid Create/Update/Delete requests and cause an unbounded number of concurrent in-flight connections/goroutines against the Legacy store with no feedback to the caller that Legacy is falling behind or failing.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/apiserver/rest/dualwriter_mode3.go`, Mode3 now performs legacy writes in detached goroutines after the unified store operation succeeds: `Create` (new `go func(){ ... d.Legacy.Create(...) }`), `Delete` (new `go func(){ ... d.Legacy.Delete(...) }`), `Update` (new `go func(){ ... d.Legacy.Update(...) }`), and `DeleteCollection` (new `go func(){ ... d.Legacy.DeleteCollection(...) }`). These goroutines are spawned per request with only a 10s timeout, but there is no semaphore/worker pool/backpressure to bound concurrent in-flight legacy operations. Because the caller gets success based on `d.Storage.*` alone, a burst of requests can create an unbounded number of concurrent goroutines/connections against Legacy storage, enabling resource exhaustion and making Legacy lag/failure invisible to the client.
